summary: Explains how entropy labels, which help MPLS routers spread traffic over parallel links, should be used with Segment Routing tunnels. Segment Routing builds long label stacks, so the document describes how to place the entropy label so load balancing still works.

eli5.summary: When a road has many lanes, cars should spread out instead of crowding one. A special tag helps routers share the load, and this says where to put the tag.

questions: what is an entropy label in segment routing
where to place entropy labels in an sr label stack
subtitle: Where to put entropy labels in a Segment Routing label stack so routers can still spread traffic over parallel paths.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over MPLS encodes a path as a stack of labels, which can be deep. An entropy label placed at the bottom may sit too deep for transit routers to read, so they cannot load-balance well.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lets the ingress router insert several pairs of an Entropy Label Indicator and an entropy label in the stack, placed using each router's advertised Entropy Readable Label Depth and the ingress router's own limit on labels it can push.
tldr.outcome: Each extra pair costs two more labels, so placement is a trade-off between load-balancing coverage and stack size. The RFC describes the criteria and a simple example algorithm rather than one fixed rule.

facts.label: ERLD if EL is not usable

today: RFC 8662 is a Proposed Standard and the data here shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It applies the entropy label mechanism of RFC 6790 to Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane described in RFC 8660.

sections.title: Entropy Labels Meet Segment Routing
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) steers a packet along a path written as an ordered list of segments. With the MPLS data plane, each segment is an LSP with a label, so the path becomes a stack of labels.

Routers spread traffic over ECMP (Equal-Cost Multipath) paths and LAGs (Link Aggregation Groups) by hashing packet fields. An entropy label (EL), from RFC 6790, lets the ingress router do the hashing once and put the result in an extra label, so transit routers need less deep packet inspection. The EL follows an Entropy Label Indicator (ELI).

This document covers the case where a label hierarchy is created at a single router, as SR requires. It follows the data-plane rules of RFC 6790 and adds guidance on where to place the labels.
sections.eli5: Routers need a quick number on each packet to decide which lane to use. The entropy label is that number, written on the front so nobody has to dig through the packet.

sections.title: Readable Depth and Maximum SID Depth
sections.content:
The Entropy Readable Label Depth (ERLD) is the number of labels a router can both read, counting from the top of the stack, and use in its load-balancing function. A router that can read N labels but does not use an EL within them MUST treat its ERLD as 0. With a single ERLD per system, an implementation MAY use the minimum across line cards or across fast and slow switching paths, at the cost of more ELI/ELs.

The RFC's Figure 2 shows five packets. A router with an ERLD of 3 can use the EL in Packet 1, one with an ERLD of 5 can use it in Packets 1 to 3, and one with an ERLD of 10 can use it in all five. A SPRING router SHOULD advertise its ERLD. To do so it MUST be entropy label capable and MUST consider an EL within its first ERLD labels.

The Maximum SID Depth (MSD) is the maximum number of labels a node can impose on a packet, of any kind. A node SHOULD advertise its MSD, and its type, to a controller so the controller leaves room for service or entropy labels. In the example topology, using Adj-SIDs only needs an MSD of 10, 11 with a service label and 13 with an ELI/EL.
sections.eli5: ERLD is how many labels from the top a router can peek at. MSD is how many labels the first router can stick on a packet. Both are like how far you can see and how much you can carry.

sections.title: Binding SIDs and Entropy Label Capability
sections.content:
A Binding SID ties a segment identifier to an existing LSP, such as an RSVP-TE tunnel, an LDP path or a SPRING path. The tail end of that LSP has its own entropy label capability, and the ingress router cannot push an ELI/EL for the Binding SID without knowing it.

So the capability SHOULD be passed between signaling domains. Each Binding SID SHOULD have its own capability, which MUST be inherited from the associated LSP. If the advertising router does not know the state of the target, it MUST NOT set the capability. An ingress node MUST NOT push an ELI/EL for a Binding SID that lacks it. This works only if the router advertising the Binding SID also does the data-plane stitching.
sections.eli5: Before you write a tag on a package, you have to know that the place it is going can read tags. If you are not sure, you leave the tag off.

sections.title: Placing Entropy Labels in the Stack
sections.content:
A single ELI/EL pair for a whole SPRING path can give poor load-balancing, because it may be too deep for some routers or absent when the stack reaches others. So multiple pairs MAY be inserted, with the same or different ELs. An insertion MUST occur only with a SPRING label advertised by a router that advertised an ERLD, or with a Binding SID that has the capability set.

Placement criteria that an implementation MAY use include the following. The list is not exhaustive.

  • ERLD value: for an adjacency segment, the ERLD of the advertising node. For a node segment, the minimum along the path if known, otherwise the tail end's ERLD.
  • Segment type: a Node SID path may need balancing anywhere along it, an adjacency-set or L2 bundle segment expects balancing at the advertiser, and a single IP link or bundle member usually does not.
  • Most routers that can balance: choose positions so the most routers that need to balance can read an EL.
  • Preference for part of the path: favor the top or the bottom of the stack.

An implementation SHOULD try to maximize load-balancing where equal-cost paths exist while minimizing the number of ELI/ELs, and SHOULD let the operator choose the criteria. Different ingress routers using different criteria does not cause an interoperability issue, though using the same criteria is better for operations.
sections.eli5: If you have only a few stickers, you put them where the helpers who need them can reach them, not all at the bottom of a tall pile.

sections.title: Worked Examples and a Simple Algorithm
sections.content:
In one example, PE1 has an MSD of 11 and can add only two ELI/EL pairs. P2, P3 and P6 have an ERLD of 3 and the others 10. A good stack puts one pair right after the adjacency-set label that P2 uses to forward and another just after the label P6 uses, because P6 has LAGs to PE2. A single regular adjacency segment at P3 is less likely to need balancing.

In a second example, three pairs would be needed for end-to-end balancing but PE1 can push only one. The provider must choose which part of the path to favor, for instance after the P6 forwarding label, or at the bottom of the stack.

The RFC's simple algorithm starts at the bottom-most EL-capable label and inserts a pair, then moves the insertion point up until the last inserted EL is below the ERLD, the ERLD is greater than 2, and the new point is EL-capable. Applied to the first use case, it yields the stack <L_N-P3, ELI, EL, L_A-L1, L_N-D, ELI, EL>.
sections.eli5: The examples show a helper who can carry only a few stickers deciding which spots on a long path matter most, and a simple recipe for picking spots.

sections.title: Options Considered and Rejected
sections.content:
The RFC documents alternatives "for historical purposes". A single EL at the bottom of the stack was rejected because many hardware implementations have a low readable label depth, so a large part of the network would lose EL balancing. An EL per segment was rejected because it needs two extra labels per tunnel label, and some hardware can push only a limited number of labels.

A reusable EL for a stack of tunnels, and an EL kept at the top of the stack, were both rejected because they would need significant changes to the label-swap operations of existing hardware. ELs at readable depths is the option that became the recommended solution, which refines it to balance pushed labels against desired entropy.
sections.eli5: The authors tried other ideas first. Some hid the tag too deep for routers to see, some needed too many tags, and some needed routers to be rebuilt, so they picked the middle way.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC notes that while data-plane limits remain, hop-by-hop load-balancing of SPRING flows needs trade-offs. Entropy labels are still seen as worthwhile because routers should not have to inspect, for example, UDP ports inside a GRE tunnel carried over a 15-label SPRING tunnel. Each ELI/EL pair adds two labels, and implementations are encouraged to balance simplicity, resource use and balancing efficiency.

On security, introducing ERLD and MSD and possibly several ELI/ELs per stack does not add considerations beyond those in RFC 6790. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Adding more tags makes the label pile taller, so use only as many as you need. Nothing here makes the network less safe than before.
